title: Huygens's Principle: Diffraction
lead: Huygens’s principle says that every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets that spread forward at the speed of the wave, and that the new wavefront is the line tangent to them all. This section uses it to explain why a mirror reflects a wave at an angle equal to the incident angle and why a wave bends toward the perpendicular when it slows down, and then to explain diffraction, the bending of a wave around the edges of an opening, which is strong when the opening is about the size of the wavelength and is why sound fills a room through a door while light casts a sharp shadow.
objectives: Discuss the propagation of transverse waves.
summary_html:
• An accurate technique for determining how and where waves propagate is given by Huygens’s principle: Every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave itself. The new wavefront is a line tangent to all of the wavelets.
  • Diffraction is the bending of a wave around the edges of an opening or other obstacle.

figures.original_caption: A transverse wave, such as an electromagnetic wave like light, as viewed from above and from the side. The direction of propagation is perpendicular to the wavefronts (or wave crests) and is represented by an arrow like a ray.

(Figure 27.5) Huygens’s principle applied to a straight wavefront. Each point on the wavefront emits a semicircular wavelet that moves a distance $s = vt$. The new wavefront is a line tangent to the wavelets. (Figure 27.6) Huygens’s principle applied to a straight wavefront striking a mirror. The wavelets shown were emitted as each point on the wavefront struck the mirror. The tangent to these wavelets shows that the new wavefront has been reflected at an angle equal to the incident angle. The direction of propagation is perpendicular to the wavefront, as shown by the downward-pointing arrows. (Figure 27.7) Huygens’s principle applied to a straight wavefront traveling from one medium to another where its speed is less. The ray bends toward the perpendicular, since the wavelets have a lower speed in the second medium.

(Figure 27.8) (a) Light passing through a doorway makes a sharp outline on the floor. Since light’s wavelength is very small compared with the size of the door, it acts like a ray. (b) Sound waves bend into all parts of the room, a wave effect, because their wavelength is similar to the size of the door. (Figure 27.9) Huygens’s principle applied to a straight wavefront striking an opening. The edges of the wavefront bend after passing through the opening, a process called diffraction. The amount of bending is more extreme for a small opening, consistent with the fact that wave characteristics are most noticeable for interactions with objects about the same size as the wavelength.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following statements is true about Huygens’s principle of secondary wavelets?

options: It can be used to explain the particle behavior of waves.
It states that each point on a wavefront can be considered a new wave source.
It can be used to find the velocity of a wave.
answer.hint: Recall what the principle says each point on a wavefront does.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the amount of bending that occurs during diffraction depends on the width of the opening through which light passes.

answer.solution: By Huygens’s principle, every point of the wavefront inside the opening is a source of wavelets. In a wide opening, most of these sources have neighbors on both sides, and their wavelets add up to a straight wavefront that goes straight on; only the few wavelets near the edges spread into the shadow, so the bending is small compared with the width of the beam. In a narrow opening, only a few wavelengths wide or less, the edges are most of the opening, and the wavelets spread out in nearly every forward direction, much as a single wavelet does. The bending is therefore greatest when the opening is about the size of the wavelength, which is why light, with its very short wavelength, shows diffraction only through very narrow slits.

exercises.prompt: How do wave effects depend on the size of the object with which the wave interacts? For example, why does sound bend around the corner of a building while light does not?

answer.solution: Wave effects such as diffraction are most noticeable when the object or opening is about the same size as the wavelength, and they become negligible when the object is much larger than the wavelength. Audible sound has wavelengths from a few centimeters to several meters, similar to the size of a doorway or the corner of a building, so it bends noticeably around them. Visible light has wavelengths of only 400 to 700 nm, millions of times smaller than a building, so it bends only by a tiny amount at the edge and behaves like a ray, casting a sharp shadow.

exercises.prompt: Under what conditions can light be modeled like a ray? Like a wave?

answer.solution: Light can be modeled as a ray when it interacts with objects and openings much larger than its wavelength, such as lenses, mirrors and doorways, because then diffraction is negligible and light travels in straight lines except where it reflects or refracts. Light must be modeled as a wave when it interacts with objects or openings comparable in size to its wavelength, such as narrow slits, fine gratings or thin films, because then diffraction and interference become noticeable.

exercises.prompt: Go outside in the sunlight and observe your shadow. It has fuzzy edges even if you do not. Is this a diffraction effect? Explain.

answer.solution: Mostly not. The Sun is not a point source: it covers about half a degree of the sky, so light from one side of the Sun reaches points that the other side cannot. Near the edge of the shadow there is a region lit by only part of the Sun, which makes the edge look fuzzy, and the farther the shadow falls from you, the wider this region is. Diffraction does occur at the edge, but because the wavelength of visible light is so small compared with your body, the bending it causes is far too small to see in an ordinary shadow.

exercises.prompt: Does Huygens’s principle apply to all types of waves?

answer.solution: Yes. Huygens’s principle depends only on each point of a wavefront acting as a source of wavelets that travel at the speed of the wave, which is true of every wave. The text says it works for all types of waves, including water waves, sound waves and light waves, and that is why diffraction, which it explains, is observed for all of them.
